title: Delhi
selection: Delhi recorded an estimated 1.999 million foreign tourist visits in 2024 (India Tourism Data Compendium 2025, Table 4.1.2) and is the busiest international gateway for arrivals from Europe and the Americas. It has three UNESCO World Heritage Sites; Qutub Minar (220,044), Humayun's Tomb (158,043) and Red Fort (79,311) are among the ten ASI monuments most visited by foreign visitors in FY 2024-25 (Table 4.2.2). v2 (2026-11-05): key facts, regions and shopping added to the state record, and 10 neighbourhood pages, from Incredible India, Delhi Tourism (DTTDC) and Wikipedia. Delhi Tourism's 'About' page predates several projects it calls under construction, so only its lasting facts are used. No prices are given.

places.name: Delhi
places.summary: India's capital: three World Heritage Sites, Old Delhi's bazaars and street food, and the country's busiest international gateway.
places.seoTitle: Delhi Travel Guide: Red Fort, Qutub Minar & Old Delhi
places.seoDescription: Plan your Delhi trip: Red Fort, Qutub Minar and Humayun's Tomb, Old Delhi food, metro and airport transfers, best season, air quality and practical tips.

images.commons: File:Front view with a clear blue sky of Humayun's Tomb.jpg
images.alt: The red sandstone and white marble Humayun's Tomb under a clear blue sky in Delhi
images.caption: Humayun's Tomb, Delhi

overview.text:
India's capital is one of its oldest cities. The Ministry of Tourism counts eight historic cities within it, each built over the ruins of the last, and three UNESCO World Heritage Sites: Shah Jahan's Red Fort, the 12th-century Qutub Minar and Humayun's Tomb, the garden mausoleum that inspired the Taj Mahal.

For most international travellers Delhi is also the start of the trip: Indira Gandhi International has been India's busiest airport since 2009, and the city is the first stop on the classic Golden Triangle with Agra and Jaipur. Give it at least two days. Spend one in Old Delhi — the Red Fort, the Jama Masjid and the lanes of Chandni Chowk — and one in New Delhi and the south, from Humayun's Tomb and India Gate to the Qutub complex.

Timing matters here more than in most cities. October to March is the comfortable season, summers are very hot, and winter brings fog and, often, heavy smog. Several big sights close one day a week, so check the visiting information below before you fix your days.

items.body: Red Fort: Shah Jahan's palace-fortress, home to the Mughal emperors for almost 200 years (closed Mondays).
Qutub Minar: the 72.5 m tower begun in 1199, surrounded by the ruins of Delhi's first mosque.
Humayun's Tomb: the first garden tomb on the subcontinent, and the model for the Taj Mahal.
Chandni Chowk: Old Delhi's spice markets, jewellers' lanes and street food.
Gurudwara Bangla Sahib: free langar served to thousands every day, open around the clock.
Spend a day in Old Delhi: the Red Fort, the Jama Masjid's southern minaret and the spice market at Khari Baoli.
See the Mughal and Sultanate monuments: Humayun's Tomb in the morning and the Qutub complex in the late afternoon.
Shop the markets — Connaught Place, Chandni Chowk, Lajpat Nagar, Khan Market and Sarojini Nagar — or buy crafts from across India at Dilli Haat.
Eat your way through Chandni Chowk's street food and sweets.
Watch the evening sound and light show at the Red Fort (not on Mondays).

best_time.text:
October to March is the season the Ministry of Tourism recommends, and it is the most comfortable time for walking around monuments. Summer starts in April and peaks in late May or early June, when heat waves are common. The monsoon arrives in late June and lasts until mid-September.

Winter has its own catch. Dense fog is common, and in the World Air Quality Report 2024 Delhi was the world's most polluted capital, with smog made worse by crop burning in neighbouring states. If you are sensitive to air pollution, check the daily air-quality index before planning a day outdoors, and consider November and December the riskiest months.

how_to_reach.text:
By air: Indira Gandhi International Airport is India's busiest and the main gateway for international visitors. The Airport Express metro line runs from the airport to New Delhi station in about 15 minutes.

By train: Delhi has five main stations — New Delhi, Old Delhi, Hazrat Nizamuddin, Anand Vihar Terminal and Sarai Rohilla. Check which one your train uses. New Delhi station sits next to Paharganj, about 2 km north of Connaught Place. Book tickets on IRCTC.

local_transport.text: The Delhi Metro is the easiest way to cover long distances: it connects most of the city and nearby towns, and the first coach of every train is reserved for women. For Old Delhi, take the metro to the edge of the old city, then walk or hire a cycle rickshaw through the lanes. Auto-rickshaws and app-based taxis fill the gaps — agree the fare or use the meter before you set off.

where_to_stay.text: Paharganj, beside New Delhi station, is the traditional budget area and convenient for early trains. Connaught Place, about 2 km south, puts you at the centre of the metro network with plenty of restaurants. Many mid-range and upscale hotels are in South Delhi, which is calmer but further from Old Delhi. If you have an early flight, a hotel near the airport line saves time.

items.body: Delhi classics: butter chicken, dal makhani, chole bhature, dahi bhalla and chaat — Delhi is also where Mughlai cuisine originated.
Chandni Chowk for street food, sweets and spices — go hungry.
Langar (a free communal meal) at Gurudwara Bangla Sahib, open to everyone.
At mosques, temples and gurdwaras, dress modestly, remove your shoes and cover your head where asked (head scarves are usually provided at gurdwaras).
Akshardham doesn't allow phones or cameras inside — leave them at the cloakroom.
At the Lotus Temple, keep silence inside the prayer hall.
Ask before photographing people, especially at places of worship.

items.body: Apply for an e-Tourist visa at least 4 days before you arrive; your passport needs at least six months' validity.

items.title: Payments
items.body: Visitors can pay by QR code with NPCI's UPI One World wallet after a passport-and-visa KYC check. Carry some cash for markets and rickshaws.

items.title: Weekly closures
items.body: The Red Fort and Akshardham close on Mondays — plan Old Delhi or Humayun's Tomb for that day.

items.title: Monument tickets

items.title: Emergency
items.body: Dial 112 for police, fire or ambulance anywhere in India.

items.title: Air quality
items.body: In winter, check the air-quality index daily; people with asthma or heart conditions should limit time outdoors on smoggy days.

items.title: Heat
items.body: From April to June, sightsee early and late, carry water and rest indoors at midday.

items.title: Crowds
items.body: Old Delhi's markets are crowded — keep valuables zipped away.

items.title: Which Delhi sights close on Mondays?
items.body: The Red Fort and Akshardham are closed on Mondays. Humayun's Tomb and the Qutub Minar open daily from sunrise to sunset.

items.title: How do I get from the airport to the city?
items.body: The Airport Express metro line reaches New Delhi station in about 15 minutes; taxis are the alternative.

items.title: When is the best time to visit Delhi?
items.body: October to March. Summers are very hot, the monsoon runs from late June to mid-September, and winter smog can be severe.

items.title: How many days do I need?
items.body: Two full days cover Old Delhi and the main monuments of New Delhi and the south.
Group sights by area: Old Delhi (Red Fort, Jama Masjid, Chandni Chowk) in one day, New Delhi and the south in another.
Use the metro to beat road traffic between areas.
Don't plan the Red Fort on a Monday.

places.name: Red Fort
places.summary: Shah Jahan's red sandstone palace-fortress in Old Delhi, a World Heritage Site and home of the Mughal emperors for almost 200 years.
places.seoTitle: Red Fort Delhi: Timings, Monday Closure & What to See
places.seoDescription: Visit the Red Fort in Old Delhi: opening hours and Monday closure, the Lahori Gate, museums inside, the evening sound and light show and nearby sights.

images.commons: File:Lahori Gate, Red Fort, Delhi, India - September 2014.jpg
images.alt: The red sandstone walls and Lahori Gate of the Red Fort in Delhi under a blue sky
images.caption: Lahori Gate, Red Fort

overview.text:
In 1639 the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan moved his court from Agra to Delhi and ordered a new palace-fortress at the heart of his new city, Shahjahanabad. The Red Fort, named for its red sandstone walls, was the residence of the Mughal emperors for almost 200 years, and the Red Fort Complex became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007.

Visits begin at the Lahori Gate and pass through the covered Meena Bazaar to the Naubat Khana, now the Indian War Memorial Museum, and on to the Diwan-i-Am and the marble pavilions of the private palaces. The Mumtaz Mahal houses the Red Fort Archaeological Museum. The fort still matters to modern India: every Independence Day the Prime Minister raises the national flag here. In 2024–25 it drew 2.88 million domestic visitors, the fourth most of any ticketed ASI monument.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: 9:30 am – 4:30 pm. Closed on Mondays.

items.title: Entrance
items.body: Through the Lahori Gate.

items.title: Sound and light show
items.body: Every evening except Mondays.

items.title: Tickets
items.body: Check the current fee on the Archaeological Survey of India's official site before you go.
Combine with the Jama Masjid and Chandni Chowk, all within walking distance.
Allow about two hours inside, more if you visit the museums.

how_to_reach.text: Take the metro to Lal Qila or Jama Masjid on the Violet Line's underground heritage stretch, or Chandni Chowk on the Yellow Line, and walk.

places.name: Qutub Minar
places.summary: A 72.5 m sandstone tower begun in 1199, the tallest masonry tower in India, at the heart of a World Heritage complex in Mehrauli.
places.seoTitle: Qutub Minar Delhi: History, Timings & the Qutub Complex
places.seoDescription: Visit the Qutub Minar, a UNESCO World Heritage Site in south Delhi: the 12th-century tower, the Iron Pillar, Alai Darwaza, opening hours and tips.

images.alt: The Qutub Minar lit up at dusk beside a domed tomb in the Qutub complex, Delhi
images.caption: Qutub Minar at dusk

images.alt: Looking up at the fluted red sandstone storeys and balconies of the Qutub Minar
images.caption: The fluted storeys of the minar

overview.text:
Standing 72.5 m high, the Qutub Minar is the tallest masonry tower in India. Qutb-ud-din Aibak, founder of the Delhi Sultanate, began it in 1199 and completed the first storey; his successor Iltutmish added three more. Built of red and buff sandstone and covered in carved bands of inscriptions, it is the centrepiece of the Qutb complex, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1993.

Give yourself time for the rest of the complex: the Quwwat ul-Islam Mosque, the Alai Darwaza gateway, the unfinished Alai Minar and the tombs of Iltutmish and Alauddin Khalji. In the courtyard, the Iron Pillar carries a 4th-century Sanskrit inscription in Brahmi script. In 2024 the Qutub Minar was India's third most visited ticketed monument for both Indian and foreign visitors.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: Sunrise to sunset; timings may vary with the season.

items.title: Tickets
items.body: Check the current fee on the Archaeological Survey of India's official site before you go.
Go in the late afternoon for warm light on the sandstone.
Allow 1.5–2 hours to see the whole complex, not just the tower.

how_to_reach.text: Qutub Minar station is on the Yellow Line, the same line as New Delhi station and Hauz Khas.

places.name: Humayun's Tomb
places.summary: The first garden tomb on the Indian subcontinent, commissioned in 1558 — and the model for the Taj Mahal.
places.seoTitle: Humayun's Tomb Delhi: History, Timings & Visitor Tips
places.seoDescription: Visit Humayun's Tomb, the UNESCO-listed Mughal garden tomb in Nizamuddin, Delhi: history, opening hours, the tombs in the complex and nearby sights.

images.alt: Humayun's Tomb seen across its fountain and garden pool in Delhi
images.caption: Humayun's Tomb from the garden

overview.text:
Humayun's Tomb was commissioned in 1558 by Empress Bega Begum, Humayun's first wife, and built by Persian architects with Indian craftsmen. It was the first garden tomb on the Indian subcontinent, set in a four-part charbagh garden, and its design inspired later Mughal tombs, culminating in the Taj Mahal. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993.

The complex is sometimes called the necropolis of the Mughals: more than 100 graves lie within it. Before the main tomb you pass Isa Khan's tomb, which predates Humayun's, and the blue-tiled Nila Gumbad. The tomb is in Nizamuddin East, near Purana Qila, and the Nizamuddin Dargah and Sunder Nursery are a short walk away. In 2024–25 it received 158,043 foreign visitors, the fourth most of any ticketed ASI monument.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: Sunrise to sunset.

items.title: Tickets
items.body: Check the current fee on the Archaeological Survey of India's official site before you go.
Combine with Sunder Nursery next door and the qawwali at Nizamuddin Dargah.
Early morning is quietest and best for photographs.
See the tomb at opening time, when the light is soft and the gardens are empty.
Walk across to Sunder Nursery's restored Mughal gardens next door.
Stay for the evening qawwali at the Nizamuddin Dargah, a short walk away.

places.name: Jama Masjid
places.summary: Shah Jahan's great mosque in Old Delhi, with a courtyard for 25,000 worshippers and minaret views over the old city.
places.seoTitle: Jama Masjid Delhi: Timings, Etiquette & Minaret Views
places.seoDescription: Visit the Jama Masjid in Old Delhi, one of India's largest mosques: history, visiting hours, dress and etiquette, and the climb up the southern minaret.

images.alt: The red sandstone courtyard and gateway of the Jama Masjid in Delhi with visitors
images.caption: The courtyard of the Jama Masjid

overview.text:
The Jama Masjid was built by Shah Jahan between 1650 and 1656 at the highest point of his new city, Shahjahanabad, and remains one of the largest mosques in India. Its red sandstone and marble courtyard can hold up to 25,000 worshippers, and it is still an active place of prayer.

For the best view of Old Delhi, climb the southern minaret. The mosque is a short walk from the Red Fort and the lanes of Chandni Chowk, so it fits easily into a day in the old city. Avoid prayer times, especially Friday midday prayers, when the mosque is busiest with worshippers.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: 7 am – 12 pm and 1:30 pm – 6:30 pm.

items.title: Dress
items.body: Cover shoulders and legs and remove your shoes before entering.
Visit after the Red Fort, then walk into Chandni Chowk for lunch.

how_to_reach.text: Jama Masjid metro station is a short walk from the mosque (Gate 1). On the Yellow Line, get off at Chawri Bazar and walk or take a cycle rickshaw.

items.body: Visitors are not let in between 12 and 1:30 pm.
Dress modestly; expect touts on the steps and decline guides you didn't ask for.

places.name: Chandni Chowk
places.summary: Shah Jahan's 17th-century boulevard, now Old Delhi's busiest market: spices, jewellery, sweets and street food.
places.seoTitle: Chandni Chowk, Old Delhi: Markets & Street Food Guide
places.seoDescription: Explore Chandni Chowk in Old Delhi: Khari Baoli spice market, Dariba Kalan's jewellers, Mughlai food and street food, and how to get around the lanes.

images.commons: File:Chandni Chowk, Old Delhi, India - September 2014.jpg
images.alt: Rickshaws and traffic beside the Chandni Chowk street sign in Old Delhi
images.caption: Chandni Chowk, Old Delhi

overview.text:
Chandni Chowk was laid out in the 17th century by Shah Jahan as the grand boulevard of his new capital; its name means 'Moonlight Square', after a pool that once reflected the moon. Today it is the crowded, noisy heart of Old Delhi and one of the city's great experiences.

Each lane has its own trade. Khari Baoli is Asia's largest wholesale spice market; Dariba Kalan, once the street of jewellers, still sells silver, pearls and ittar (natural perfume). Food is the other reason to come — from long-established Mughlai restaurants to street food and sweets. Go with time and an appetite, and see it on foot or by cycle rickshaw.

items.body: Mornings are calmer; many shops open late morning.
Take the metro to the old city rather than driving — roads here are slow.
Keep bags closed and valuables out of sight in the crowds.

how_to_reach.text: Chandni Chowk metro station (Yellow Line) is linked to Old Delhi railway station by underground walkways. Chawri Bazar, one stop away, is handy for the Jama Masjid end.

Karim's and Al Jawahar near the Jama Masjid for kebabs and biryani
Kake Di Hatti for chhole bhature
Chaat and aloo tikki from street stalls

places.name: India Gate
places.summary: Lutyens's 42 m war memorial arch on Kartavya Path, a favourite place for an evening walk.
places.seoTitle: India Gate Delhi: History, Visiting Hours & Nearby Sights
places.seoDescription: Visit India Gate in New Delhi, the war memorial designed by Lutyens: its history, when to go, evening lights and nearby sights like the National War Memorial.

images.commons: File:India Gate, New Delhi from West.jpg
images.alt: The sandstone arch of India Gate seen across the lawns from the west, New Delhi
images.caption: India Gate from the west

overview.text:
India Gate is a 42 m sandstone arch designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens as a memorial to the 70,000 Indian soldiers who died in the First World War and the Third Anglo-Afghan War. The Duke of Connaught laid the foundation stone in 1921, and the Viceroy, Lord Irwin, dedicated it in 1931.

It stands on Kartavya Path, the ceremonial avenue where the Republic Day parade is held each January. The surrounding lawns are open all day and popular with families in the evening, when the arch is lit up, though some areas close after dark. The National War Memorial is a short walk away.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: Open throughout the day; some areas are closed to visitors after dark.

items.title: Entry
items.body: No ticket is needed to walk around the lawns.
Come at dusk and walk over to the National War Memorial for the Retreat ceremony.
The National Museum and National Gallery of Modern Art are close.

places.name: Lotus Temple
places.summary: Delhi's Bahá'í House of Worship: 27 marble petals around a silent prayer hall open to people of every faith.
places.seoTitle: Lotus Temple Delhi: Timings, Etiquette & Architecture
places.seoDescription: Visit the Lotus Temple, Delhi's Bahá'í House of Worship: opening hours in summer and winter, silence in the prayer hall, and its 27-petal marble design.

images.alt: The white marble petals of the Lotus Temple above its blue reflecting pools in Delhi
images.caption: The Lotus Temple

overview.text:
The Lotus Temple is a Bahá'í House of Worship that opened in December 1986. As at every Bahá'í temple, anyone may enter regardless of religion. Its shape is unmistakable: 27 free-standing marble petals in clusters of three, with nine doors leading into a central hall for up to 2,500 people, surrounded by nine reflecting pools.

Inside there are no idols or sermons. At set times there are readings from the sacred texts of many faiths; at other times visitors may pray or meditate in silence. Expect a short queue at busy times, and keep your voice down in the hall.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: 9:30 am – 7 pm in summer; 9:30 am – 5:30 pm in winter.

items.title: Inside
items.body: Silence in the prayer hall; shoes are removed before entering.

images.caption: Swaminarayan Akshardham

overview.text: Swaminarayan Akshardham is a huge temple complex dedicated to Bhagwan Swaminarayan, built of Italian Carrara marble and pink sandstone. Beyond the temple itself there is a boat ride through Indian history, the Hall of Values exhibition and, after dark, the Sahaj Anand Water Show. It is about half a kilometre from Akshardham metro station. Phones and cameras are not allowed inside, and it is closed on Mondays.

places.name: Gurudwara Bangla Sahib
places.summary: Central Delhi's best-known Sikh gurdwara, with a sacred pool and a free community kitchen open to everyone.
places.seoTitle: Gurudwara Bangla Sahib Delhi: Langar, Etiquette & Timings
places.seoDescription: Visit Gurudwara Bangla Sahib in central Delhi: its history, the free langar served daily, the sarovar, etiquette for visitors and opening hours.

images.alt: The white gurdwara with a golden dome reflected in the sarovar at Gurudwara Bangla Sahib
images.caption: The sarovar at Gurudwara Bangla Sahib

overview.text:
Gurudwara Bangla Sahib stands on the site of a palace belonging to Raja Jai Singh, where the eighth Sikh Guru, Guru Har Krishan, stayed in 1664 and cared for the sick during an epidemic. Today its white marble building and golden domes rise above a large sarovar, or sacred pool.

The gurdwara welcomes visitors of every faith around the clock. In the langar hall, volunteers serve free meals to thousands of people every day, whatever their caste, creed or status — sitting down to eat together is the best way to understand the Sikh principle of equality. Cover your head, remove your shoes and wash your feet before entering.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: Open 24 hours.

items.title: Etiquette
items.body: Cover your head (scarves are available), remove your shoes and don't bring tobacco or alcohol.

overview.text:
Old Delhi is Shahjahanabad, the walled city Shah Jahan made his capital in 1648; it stayed the Mughal capital until 1857. The Red Fort, the Jama Masjid and the Digambar Jain Lal Mandir are its great landmarks, and Chandni Chowk, laid out in the 17th century, still runs through its heart.

Today it is known for bazaars and street food: Khari Baoli is Asia's largest wholesale spice market, and Dariba Kalan sells jewellery and ittar. Cycle rickshaws are the easiest way through the narrow lanes. By the Yamuna, Raj Ghat marks where Mahatma Gandhi was cremated in 1948, and Feroz Shah Kotla's ruins hold an Ashokan pillar.

items.body: Visit the Red Fort (closed Mondays).
Climb the Jama Masjid's southern minaret.
Walk Khari Baoli and Dariba Kalan.
Eat your way down Chandni Chowk.
Pay respects at Raj Ghat.

how_to_reach.text: The metro reaches Chandni Chowk; take a cycle rickshaw through the lanes. Old Delhi railway station is in the walled city.

overview.text:
Connaught Place, officially Rajiv Chowk, was built between 1929 and 1933 to Robert Tor Russell's design as the showpiece commercial centre of New Delhi. Its white colonnaded circles are still the city's main hub for offices, shopping, restaurants and nightlife.

A short walk away on Hailey Road, Agrasen ki Baoli is a 60-m stepwell with 108 steps, probably repaired in the Tughlaq or Lodi era. New Delhi railway station is about 2 km north.

items.body: Walk the inner and outer circles.
Go down the steps of Agrasen ki Baoli.
Eat and drink in the colonnades in the evening.

where_to_stay.text: Connaught Place is New Delhi's central business and shopping hub, with metro lines meeting at Rajiv Chowk — a convenient, if busier and pricier, base. Beware of private 'tourist offices' here that claim to be official.

overview.text:
Lutyens' Delhi is the capital the British built from the late 1910s to the 1930s, largely to Edwin Lutyens's designs. Its spine is a ceremonial axis — today Kartavya Path — running from India Gate, the First World War memorial arch, up Raisina Hill to Rashtrapati Bhavan; the Republic Day parade marches along it every 26 January.

The National Museum, with over 200,000 works including the 4,500-year-old Dancing Girl of Harappa, is just off the avenue. Purana Qila, Humayun's 16th-century citadel, stands on Mathura Road.

items.body: Walk Kartavya Path from India Gate.
Visit the National War Memorial.
See the Dancing Girl at the National Museum.
Explore Purana Qila and its museum.

overview.text:
Nizamuddin is named after the 13th-century Sufi saint whose dargah draws thousands of pilgrims every week; it is known for its evening qawwali, and the poet Amir Khusrau is buried at its entrance.

Around it lies Delhi's green lung. Humayun's Tomb, the first garden tomb in the subcontinent, is a short walk away, and next to it Sunder Nursery, a 90-acre Mughal-era garden, reopened in 2018 with 15 monuments and over 300 kinds of trees.

items.body: Hear qawwali at the dargah in the evening.
Visit Humayun's Tomb.
Walk Sunder Nursery.
Continue to Lodi Gardens.

overview.text:
Lodi Gardens, 90 acres on Lodi Road between Khan Market and Safdarjung's Tomb, holds rare 15th- and 16th-century tombs of the Sayyid and Lodi dynasties — Muhammad Shah's, Sikandar Lodi's, the Bara Gumbad and the Shisha Gumbad — and is a favourite place for morning walks. It was landscaped in 1936 as Lady Willingdon Park and renamed after independence.

Khan Market, set up in 1951 for refugees from the North-West Frontier Province, is a short walk away, and the India Habitat Centre hosts cultural events nearby.

items.body: Walk Lodi Gardens early in the morning.
See the Bara Gumbad and Sikandar Lodi's tomb.
Browse Khan Market's bookshops and cafes.

overview.text:
Hauz Khas — the 'royal tank' — is named after the reservoir Alauddin Khalji built to supply his city of Siri. The tank and its buildings are now the Hauz Khas Complex, ringed by some of Delhi's largest green spaces, the Deer Park and Rose Garden.

With easy metro access and plenty of hostels and cafes, it has become a popular base for young and budget travellers exploring South Delhi. Its history goes back further than the cafes suggest: known then as Hauz-e-Alai, it is where Ghazi Malik defeated Khusro Khan in 1320.

Spend a morning in the Deer Park.
Eat at the village cafes.

where_to_stay.text: Hauz Khas has guesthouses, cafés and easy metro access, making it a popular base for visitors who want to be in south Delhi.

overview.text:
Mehrauli is held to be Delhi's oldest continuously inhabited village, founded by the Tomars, and it was the capital of the first Delhi Sultanate. The 72.5-m Qutub Minar, begun in 1199, rises above it.

Beside the minar, the 200-acre Mehrauli Archaeological Park holds more than 50 monuments: Balban's tomb, with India's first true arch and dome, the Jamali Kamali mosque and tomb, and Rajon ki Baoli, a 16th-century stepwell. The dargah of Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki hosts the annual Phoolwalon-ki-Sair festival.

items.body: See the Qutub Minar and the Iron Pillar.
Walk the Archaeological Park to Jamali Kamali and Rajon ki Baoli.
Visit the dargah of Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki.

overview.text:
Paharganj, just west of New Delhi railway station, is packed with budget hotels, lodges, dhabas and shops, and has long been the backpacker district. It is convenient for early trains.

It also has a poor record for women's safety and is known for scams and drug dealing, and many backpackers now base themselves in South Delhi instead. Connaught Place is about 2 km away.

items.title: Scams and safety
items.body: Paharganj is known for scams and drug dealing and has a poor record on women's safety — stay alert, especially at night.

how_to_reach.text: New Delhi railway station is next door; the Airport Express runs from there to the airport in about 15 minutes.

where_to_stay.text: Paharganj, beside New Delhi station, is Delhi's classic backpacker area of cheap hotels and cafés, handy for early trains. It also has a poor safety record, especially for women — choose a well-reviewed place on a main street and avoid wandering late.

overview.text:
Majnu-ka-Tilla, on the banks of the Yamuna in north Delhi, grew from a Tibetan refugee camp on land the government allotted in 1960. Still home to Tibetan families, it is also called Samyeling, with a monastery, shops and cafes in its narrow lanes.

Its name comes from the Sufi Majnu, who ferried people across the river and met Guru Nanak here in 1505; the gurdwara that marks the spot is one of Delhi's oldest Sikh shrines, on an estate given by Ranjit Singh.

Visit the monastery.

Visit the gurdwara.

overview.text:
Aerocity is the hospitality district of Indira Gandhi International Airport, planned for 16 luxury hotels and offices, with quick access to the terminals and a position between Delhi and Gurgaon.

Its station is on the Airport Express line, which reaches New Delhi station in about 15 minutes, so it suits travellers with early flights or a single night in transit.

The airport itself, at Palam about 15 km south-west of New Delhi station, has been India's busiest by passengers since 2009. A second airport, Noida International at Jewar in Uttar Pradesh, opened its first phase in March 2026 — check which one your flight uses.

where_to_stay.text: Aerocity is the airport's hotel district, on the Airport Express metro line — the obvious choice for early flights or a short stopover.

places.name: Safdarjung's Tomb
places.summary: The last great Mughal garden tomb, built in 1754 for Nawab Safdarjung, a calm alternative to Humayun's Tomb near Lodhi Garden.
places.seoTitle: Safdarjung's Tomb Delhi: History, Metro & Visit Tips
places.seoDescription: Visit Safdarjung's Tomb, the last Mughal garden tomb (1754): what to see, its ornate gateway, nearest metro at Jor Bagh, and how to pair it with Lodhi Garden.

images.alt: Safdarjung's Tomb with its white dome rising beyond a long water channel lined with palm trees
images.caption: Safdarjung's Tomb from the gateway

overview.text:
Safdarjung's Tomb was built in 1754 for Nawab Safdarjung, in the late Mughal style. It was the first time someone outside the imperial family built himself a tomb and garden on this scale — a sign of how weak the emperors had become.

It is also the last of the great Mughal garden tombs, laid out like Humayun's Tomb and the Taj Mahal: a walled garden with water channels leading to a domed mausoleum on a high terrace. Look closely at the two-storey gateway as you enter — its plastered façade is richly decorated.

how_to_reach.text: Take the Delhi Metro to Jor Bagh; the tomb is close to the station. Lodhi Garden and Khan Market are a short ride away, so the three make an easy half day.

items.body: Come in the morning or late afternoon, when the light on the dome is softest and the garden is quiet.
Pair it with Lodhi Garden next door for a relaxed half day of Sayyid, Lodi and Mughal tombs.

places.name: Purana Qila
places.summary: Humayun's 16th-century citadel on Mathura Road, rebuilt by Sher Shah Suri, with a mosque, the Sher Mandal and finds from 1000 BC.
places.seoTitle: Purana Qila Delhi: Timings, History & Sound and Light
places.seoDescription: Visit Purana Qila (Old Fort): 7 am–6 pm, the Bara Darwaza, Qila-i Kuhna Mosque, Sher Mandal, site museum, evening sound and light show and nearby sights.

images.alt: The red sandstone octagonal Sher Mandal tower on a lawn inside Purana Qila under a cloudy sky
images.caption: Sher Mandal, Purana Qila

overview.text:
Purana Qila — the Old Fort — stands on Mathura Road near Pragati Maidan. It was the inner citadel of Dinpanah, the city Humayun began in the 16th century, Delhi's sixth. Sher Shah Suri seized it, strengthened it and renamed it Shergarh, before Humayun returned 15 years later and took it back.

Enter through the western Bara Darwaza; the walls run for nearly 1.5 km and rise 18 m. Inside, Sher Shah's Qila-i Kuhna Mosque of 1541 is a fine pre-Mughal building, and the octagonal Sher Mandal is the tower from which Humayun fell to his death. The small archaeological museum shows how long people have lived here — its finds include Painted Grey Ware from 1000 BC.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: 7 am – 6 pm.

items.title: Evening show
items.body: A sound and light show on Delhi's seven cities runs after sunset — check the schedule locally.

items.title: Tickets
items.body: ASI tickets can be booked online through ONDC apps (₹5 off for Indian visitors, ₹50 off for foreign visitors).
Combine it with the National Crafts Museum next door, then Humayun's Tomb and Sunder Nursery a few minutes south.
Stay on for the evening sound and light show if it's running.

places.name: Agrasen ki Baoli
places.summary: A 60-metre stone stepwell with 108 steps on Hailey Road, a short walk from Connaught Place — and Delhi's favourite 'haunted' photo spot.
places.seoTitle: Agrasen ki Baoli: Delhi's Stepwell Near Connaught Place
places.seoDescription: Agrasen ki Baoli, the 14th-century stepwell near Connaught Place: 108 steps, the whale-back mosque, the ghost stories, photography tips and how to get there.

images.alt: Looking down the stone steps of Agrasen ki Baoli between tiers of arched niches
images.caption: Agrasen ki Baoli

overview.text:
Hidden between office blocks on Hailey Road, Agrasen ki Baoli is a stone stepwell 60 m long and 15 m wide, with 108 steps leading down past tiers of arched niches. Local legend credits King Agrasen, but the present structure was probably repaired in the Tughlaq or Lodi era, in the 14th or 15th century. It is protected by the Archaeological Survey of India.

The baoli has a reputation as haunted, but that is folklore with no evidence behind it — today it is simply a favourite with photographers. At the top, look for the small ruined mosque with its unusual whale-back roof and red pillars.

how_to_reach.text: It is a short walk from Connaught Place, so you can fit it into a CP lunch or shopping trip.

items.body: Go early in the day for the best light down the steps and fewer people.
Combine it with Connaught Place and Jantar Mantar, both close by.

places.name: Lodhi Garden
places.summary: A 90-acre park of 15th–16th-century Sayyid and Lodi tombs, lawns, a lake and a bonsai park, beside Khan Market.
places.seoTitle: Lodhi Garden Delhi: Tombs, Walks & What to See
places.seoDescription: Lodhi Garden guide: the tombs of Muhammad Shah and Sikandar Lodi, Bara and Sheesh Gumbad, the glass house and bonsai park, plus Khan Market nearby.

images.alt: Bara Gumbad's domed tomb and mosque beyond a lawn where people sit on picnic mats
images.caption: Bara Gumbad, Lodhi Garden

overview.text:
Lodhi Garden is where New Delhi goes to walk. It began as a 15th-century burial ground of the Lodi rulers and holds the tomb of Muhammad Shah Sayyid, built in 1444, the tomb of Sikandar Lodi, the great Bara Gumbad and the Sheesh Gumbad, whose interior once glittered with reflective tiles.

Lady Willingdon landscaped the grounds in 1936, and in 1968 Garrett Eckbo and Joseph Allen Stein added a glass house, a lake with fountains, a bonsai park and a rose garden. Khan Market is a short distance away, and Safdarjung's Tomb and Humayun's Tomb are within easy reach.

items.body: Morning and early evening are the best times: cooler, with locals out walking.
Finish with lunch or coffee at Khan Market, a short distance away.

places.name: Sunder Nursery
places.summary: A restored 90-acre Mughal garden beside Humayun's Tomb, with 15 monuments, lawns and walks, reopened in 2018.
places.seoTitle: Sunder Nursery Delhi: Mughal Gardens Next to Humayun's Tomb
places.seoDescription: Sunder Nursery, the 16th-century Azim Bagh restored by the Aga Khan Trust: 15 monuments including Lakkarwala Burj, lawns and how to pair it with Humayun's Tomb.

images.alt: A long lawn with low hedges leading to the domed Lakkarwala Burj
images.caption: Lakkarwala Burj, Sunder Nursery

overview.text:
Sunder Nursery was the Mughal Azim Bagh, a 16th-century garden on the old Grand Trunk Road right beside Humayun's Tomb. Spread over 90 acres, it holds fifteen heritage monuments — six of them part of the UNESCO-listed Humayun's Tomb site — including Sundarwala Burj, Sundarwala Mahal and Lakkarwala Burj.

The Aga Khan Trust restored it from 2007 as part of the Nizamuddin urban renewal project, and it reopened as a heritage park on 21 February 2018. It is one of the most pleasant green spaces in Delhi for a slow walk or a picnic.

items.body: Visit Humayun's Tomb first thing, then cross to Sunder Nursery for a long walk.
The Nizamuddin Dargah, with its evening qawwali, is a short walk away.

places.name: Jantar Mantar
places.summary: Maharaja Jai Singh II's 1724 open-air observatory of giant masonry instruments, near Connaught Place.
places.seoTitle: Jantar Mantar Delhi: The 1724 Observatory Explained
places.seoDescription: Jantar Mantar in New Delhi: Jai Singh II's 1724 observatory, the Samrat Yantra sundial and other instruments, nearest metro and what to combine it with.

images.alt: Red-painted masonry astronomical instruments with staircases and curved walls at Jantar Mantar
images.caption: Jantar Mantar instruments

overview.text:
Jantar Mantar was built in 1724 by Maharaja Jai Singh II of Jaipur: an open-air observatory of 13 architectural instruments for tracking the sun, moon and stars. The main ones are the Samrat, Jai Prakash, Ram and Misra yantras. The Samrat Yantra — the 'supreme instrument' — is a giant triangular sundial.

It sits just off Connaught Place, so it's an easy, short stop between the CP shops, Agrasen ki Baoli and Gurudwara Bangla Sahib. Allow about an hour, and come on a sunny day — the instruments only work when they cast a shadow.

how_to_reach.text: Patel Chowk metro station is the closest; Gurudwara Bangla Sahib is served by the same station.

items.body: Go when the sun is out — the instruments only make sense when they cast shadows.
Allow about an hour, then walk on to Connaught Place.

places.name: Rashtrapati Bhavan
places.summary: The President's 340-room Lutyens palace on Raisina Hill: book a tour of the state rooms, the museum, the Saturday Change of Guard or Amrit Udyan in spring.
places.seoTitle: Rashtrapati Bhavan Tour: Booking, Timings & Amrit Udyan
places.seoDescription: How to visit Rashtrapati Bhavan: main building tours (Tue–Sun), the museum, the Saturday Change of Guard, Amrit Udyan's February–March season, gates and metro.

images.alt: View along the ceremonial avenue towards Rashtrapati Bhavan's dome between the sandstone Secretariat blocks
images.caption: Raisina Hill and Rashtrapati Bhavan

overview.text:
Rashtrapati Bhavan, the official home of the President of India, was designed by Edwin Lutyens and finished in 1929 as the Viceroy's House. The H-shaped mansion has 340 rooms on four floors, in a 330-acre estate on Raisina Hill.

You can visit in several ways, all booked through the official Visit Rashtrapati Bhavan site. The main building tour (Circuit One) takes you through the Forecourt and the state rooms. The Rashtrapati Bhavan Museum tells the building's story with interactive displays. On Saturdays the President's Bodyguard — raised in 1773, the Indian Army's senior-most regiment — performs the Change of Guard with an equestrian display. And every February–March the gardens, now called Amrit Udyan, open to the public.

items.title: Main building
items.body: Tuesday–Sunday, 9:30 am – 4:30 pm; last entry 4 pm. Enter by Gate 38 on Church Road.

items.title: Museum
items.body: Tuesday–Sunday, 9:30 am – 5 pm; last entry 4 pm. Phase II has been closed since 6 October 2025.

items.title: Change of Guard
items.body: Saturdays except gazetted holidays; 8–9 am from 7 November 2026. Registration ₹50 a person, online.

items.title: Amrit Udyan
items.body: Open each February–March. Online booking is compulsory and closes at 10 am the day before.

how_to_reach.text: Central Secretariat metro station is about 1 km from Gate 38, the entry for the main building tour and the Change of Guard.

items.body: Tour the state rooms of the main building (Circuit One).
See the interactive Rashtrapati Bhavan Museum.
Watch the Saturday Change of Guard by the President's Bodyguard.
In February–March, walk Amrit Udyan's 15 acres of Mughal-style gardens, with a children's garden around a 225-year-old sheesham tree.
Book online before you go — slots are limited and booking for Amrit Udyan closes the morning before.
Carry the ID you booked with.
Combine a morning tour with the National Museum and India Gate on the same side of town.

images.caption: Pradhanmantri Sangrahalaya

overview.text:
The Pradhanmantri Sangrahalaya at Teen Murti House is a museum of India since Independence told through its Prime Ministers — every one of them, with their lives and the work of their governments. It opened on 14 April 2022 at Teen Murti House, Jawaharlal Nehru's former residence, and tells the story of India's democracy over 75 years through each leader's life, speeches and decisions.

Allow two to three hours. It is closed on Mondays and gazetted holidays, and tickets (₹100) can be bought online in advance, which saves queuing. It sits in leafy Chanakyapuri, so it combines well with the National Rail Museum on the same side of the city.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: 10 am – 6 pm. Closed on Mondays and gazetted holidays.

items.title: Ticket
items.body: ₹100 a person (add-ons extra); online tickets available.

places.name: Raj Ghat
places.summary: The black-marble memorial by the Yamuna where Mahatma Gandhi was cremated in 1948, with an eternal flame and quiet gardens.
places.seoTitle: Raj Ghat Delhi: Gandhi Memorial Timings & Visit
places.seoDescription: Raj Ghat, Mahatma Gandhi's memorial by the Yamuna: the black marble platform and eternal flame, 7 am–6 pm, Friday prayers, and the nearby Gandhi museum.

images.commons: File:Raj Ghat – Memorial of Mahatma Gandhi.jpg
images.alt: The black marble platform at Raj Ghat decorated with marigolds, with the eternal flame lamp at one end
images.caption: Raj Ghat

overview.text:
Raj Ghat is the simple, moving memorial to Mahatma Gandhi beside the Yamuna. A black-marble platform marks the spot where he was cremated on 31 January 1948, with an eternal flame at one end, set in gardens designed by Vanu G. Bhuta and planted by Alick Percy-Lancaster.

Prayer meetings are held on Fridays, and Martyrs' Day is marked here on 30 January, the anniversary of his assassination. The National Gandhi Museum is nearby, and the Red Fort is a short ride away, so Raj Ghat fits easily into a day in Old Delhi.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: 7 am – 6 pm.

items.title: Prayers
items.body: Fridays; Martyrs' Day on 30 January.
Take your shoes off before you step onto the memorial platform, as visitors do.
Combine it with the National Gandhi Museum nearby and the Red Fort.

places.name: Mehrauli Archaeological Park
places.summary: 200 acres of ruins beside the Qutub Minar spanning 1,000 years — Balban's tomb, Jamali Kamali, Rajon ki Baoli and the Jahaz Mahal.
places.seoTitle: Mehrauli Archaeological Park: Heritage Walk Guide
places.seoDescription: Walk the Mehrauli Archaeological Park next to the Qutub Minar: 50+ monuments from Lal Kot to the Lodis — Balban's tomb, Jamali Kamali, Rajon ki Baoli and Jahaz Mahal.

images.commons: File:Jamali Kamali Mosque New Delhi, India.jpg
images.alt: The weathered stone façade and dome of the Jamali Kamali mosque among trees
images.caption: Jamali Kamali Mosque

overview.text:
Right next to the Qutub Minar, the 200-acre Mehrauli Archaeological Park holds more than 50 monuments and is the only part of Delhi with 1,000 years of continuous settlement — from the Tomar Rajputs' Lal Kot of 1060 through the Sultanate and Mughal eras to the British Raj.

Look for the tomb of Balban (around 1287), with India's first true arch and dome; the Jamali Kamali mosque and tomb (1526–35); Rajon ki Baoli, the 'stepwell of the masons'; and the Lodi-era Jahaz Mahal, a pleasure pavilion shaped like a boat.

items.body: Walk it straight after the Qutub Minar — it's a short walk away — and wear good shoes for uneven paths.
Go in the morning in the cooler months; there's little shade at midday in summer.

places.name: Tughlaqabad Fort
places.summary: The vast, unfinished 1321 citadel of Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq in south Delhi — massive walls, 13 surviving gates and a cursed legend.
places.seoTitle: Tughlaqabad Fort Delhi: History, Timings & Visit Tips
places.seoDescription: Explore Tughlaqabad Fort (1321): Delhi's third city, its massive walls and gates, Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq's tomb, Adilabad Fort, timings and tips.

images.alt: Ruined stone bastions of Tughlaqabad Fort overlooking scrubland and a long arched causeway
images.caption: Tughlaqabad Fort ruins

overview.text:
Tughlaqabad was Delhi's third city, after Lal Kot and Siri, built in 1321 by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, founder of the Tughlaq dynasty. Today it is a vast, largely untouched ruin — massive stone walls snaking over rough ground, with 13 of its original 52 gates still standing.

Legend says the Sufi saint Nizamuddin Auliya cursed the city to lie deserted after a quarrel over workers. Opposite the fort, Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq's red sandstone tomb holds his grave, and Adilabad Fort lies about 1 km to the east.

items.title: Terrain
items.body: Large and rough — wear sturdy shoes and carry water.
Visit in the cooler months and in daylight; the site is big and exposed.
Pair it with the Qutub Minar and Mehrauli on the same day.

places.name: Dilli Haat
places.summary: Delhi Tourism's open-air crafts and food bazaar at INA, where stalls from different states rotate — good for souvenirs and regional food.
places.seoTitle: Dilli Haat INA: Timings, Metro, Food & Crafts
places.seoDescription: Dilli Haat guide: rotating craft stalls from across India, regional food, 11 am–9 pm, INA metro, and the Pitampura and Janakpuri sites.

images.alt: The red arched Dilli Haat INA sign over a busy paved entrance plaza
images.caption: Dilli Haat, INA

overview.text:
Dilli Haat is a permanent village-style bazaar run by Delhi Tourism. Opened in 1994, it has three sites — opposite INA market, at Pitampura and at Janakpuri — where craft stalls from different states rotate, so there's always something new: textiles, metalwork, pottery and more.

It's also one of the easiest places to try regional food from across India — Rajasthani thalis, Bengali sweets, Kashmiri kebabs — in one place. The INA site, on the metro, is the most convenient for visitors; it opens late morning and stays open into the evening.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: 11 am – 9 pm.

items.title: Metro
items.body: INA (Dilli Haat INA), Netaji Subhash Place (Pitampura), Janakpuri East (Janakpuri).
Go in the late afternoon and stay for dinner from the state food stalls.
Compare prices between stalls before you buy.

places.name: National Rail Museum
places.summary: Eleven acres of locomotives and royal saloons in Chanakyapuri, with the Fairy Queen, a toy-train ride and simulators — great with children.
places.seoTitle: National Rail Museum Delhi: Timings, Tickets & Toy Train
places.seoDescription: National Rail Museum, Chanakyapuri: the Fairy Queen steam engine, royal saloons, mini-train ride, simulators, 10 am–5 pm (closed Mondays), ₹10 tickets.

images.commons: File:An old carriage at National Rail Museum, New Delhi 2.jpg
images.alt: A restored wooden railway carriage on display under trees at the National Rail Museum
images.caption: A historic carriage at the National Rail Museum

overview.text:
The National Rail Museum, opened in 1977 in the diplomatic enclave of Chanakyapuri, spreads over 11 acres of locomotives, coaches and royal saloons. Look out for the Fairy Queen, the world's oldest working steam locomotive, and the 1907 Patiala State Monorail. Children love the mini-train ride around the yard and the coach simulators.

Most of the collection is outdoors, laid out like a railway yard under the trees, so it's best on a cool morning. Tickets cost just ₹10 for adults and ₹3 for children, and the museum is closed on Mondays.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: 10 am – 5 pm. Closed on Mondays and national holidays.

items.title: Ticket
items.body: ₹10 adults, ₹3 children.

how_to_reach.text: Lok Kalyan Marg and Jor Bagh are the nearest metro stations; take an auto or cab for the last stretch.

places.name: National War Memorial
places.summary: India's memorial to its fallen soldiers beside India Gate: concentric circles, the Amar Jawan Jyoti and a daily Retreat ceremony. Free entry.
places.seoTitle: National War Memorial Delhi: Timings & Retreat Ceremony
places.seoDescription: National War Memorial next to India Gate: free entry, the Amar Chakra and Param Yodha Sthal, seasonal opening hours, the daily Retreat and Sunday Change of Guard.

images.alt: The tall obelisk of the Amar Chakra at the centre of the circular National War Memorial plaza
images.caption: Amar Chakra, National War Memorial

overview.text:
The National War Memorial, opened on 25 February 2019 beside India Gate, honours Indian soldiers who have died in war. It is laid out as concentric circles: at the centre the Amar Chakra, with an eternal flame on an obelisk, and around it the circles of bravery, sacrifice and protection. The Amar Jawan Jyoti, lit under India Gate in 1972, was moved here in January 2022.

In the Param Yodha Sthal stand bronze statues of the 21 recipients of the Param Vir Chakra, India's highest award for gallantry.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: 9 am – 7:30 pm (November–March); 9 am – 8:30 pm (April–October).

items.title: Entry
items.body: Free.

items.title: Ceremonies
items.body: Retreat every evening; on Sundays a Change of Guard and band display come first.
Come in the evening for the Retreat ceremony — Sunday is the best day.
India Gate is right next door; walk between the two.

places.name: National Museum
places.summary: India's national museum on Janpath: 200,000 works from the Harappan Dancing Girl to Mughal paintings. Closed Mondays.
places.seoTitle: National Museum Delhi: Timings, Highlights & Metro
places.seoDescription: National Museum, Janpath: highlights like the Dancing Girl of Harappa, guided tours, 10 am–6 pm (closed Mondays and national holidays), nearest metro.

images.alt: The curved sandstone and glass façade of the National Museum around its inner courtyard
images.caption: National Museum, New Delhi

overview.text:
Established in 1949 and housed on Janpath, the National Museum covers India's art and history from prehistory to modern times. Its collection runs to over 200,000 works — the 4,500-year-old bronze Dancing Girl of Harappa is its most famous piece — though only a fraction is on display at any time.

The museum runs guided tours, workshops and cultural programmes, and its audio-visual displays make it a good stop with children. Allow at least two hours, and note that it is closed on Mondays and national holidays. It sits on Janpath in the heart of Lutyens' Delhi, a short walk from India Gate.

items.title: Opening hours
items.body: 10 am – 6 pm. Closed on Mondays and national holidays.

how_to_reach.text: Udyog Bhawan metro station is close by. India Gate and Rashtrapati Bhavan are on the same avenue.

places.name: Old Delhi food walk
places.summary: Chaat, parathas, kebabs and biryani through Chandni Chowk and around the Jama Masjid — Delhi's street-food heartland.
places.seoTitle: Old Delhi Food Walk: Chandni Chowk Street Food Guide
places.seoDescription: An Old Delhi food walk: chaat, Paranthe Wali Gali, Karim's kebabs, Jama Masjid biryani and Moti Mahal butter chicken — routes, timing and food-safety tips.

images.alt: A street-food stall in Old Delhi piled with fried snacks, puris and pans of chole
images.caption: Street food, Old Delhi

overview.text:
Chandni Chowk is Delhi's street-food centre: zesty chaat, aloo tikki, kebabs, flaky parathas and samosas, from the lane of Paranthe Wali Gali to Karim's near the Jama Masjid. Make a slow loop through Old Delhi on foot — start at the Jama Masjid end for biryani at Al Jawahar, work through the parathas and chaat, and try chhole bhature at Kake Di Hatti. Moti Mahal in nearby Daryaganj is famous for butter chicken.

Eat where food is cooked fresh in front of you, and drink bottled water — tap water is usually not safe.

items.title: Where
items.body: Chandni Chowk and around the Jama Masjid

items.title: Allow
items.body: 2–3 hours, on foot

items.title: Best time
items.body: Late morning to evening; Old Delhi's lanes are quiet early
Go hungry and share plates so you can try more.
Take the metro to Chawri Bazar or Jama Masjid rather than a car — traffic in Old Delhi is slow.

places.name: Cycle-rickshaw ride through Old Delhi
places.summary: Ride a cycle rickshaw through Chandni Chowk's lanes and bazaars — spices at Khari Baoli, jewellery and ittar at Dariba Kalan.
places.seoTitle: Chandni Chowk Rickshaw Ride: Old Delhi's Bazaars
places.seoDescription: Take a cycle-rickshaw ride through Old Delhi: how to start from Chawri Bazar metro, the bazaars of Khari Baoli and Dariba Kalan, and tips on fares.

images.commons: File:Cycle Rickshaw - Chandni Chowk Road - Delhi 2014-05-13 3517.JPG
images.alt: A man pedals a blue-canopied cycle rickshaw carrying passengers along Chandni Chowk road
images.caption: Cycle rickshaw, Chandni Chowk

overview.text:
A cycle rickshaw is the most fun way through Old Delhi's narrow lanes — slow enough to see everything, small enough to squeeze through. Start from Chawri Bazar metro on the Yellow Line, where rickshaws wait, and ride through the bazaars: Khari Baoli, Asia's largest wholesale spice market, and Dariba Kalan for jewellery and ittar.

It works well before or after the Jama Masjid, which is a short ride from Chawri Bazar, and you can hop off to eat along the way. Go in the morning before the lanes are at their busiest, and keep the ride to an hour or so — the riders work hard in the heat.

items.body: Agree the fare and the route before you set off.
Keep bags on your lap and phones zipped away in the crowds.

places.name: Red Fort sound and light show
places.summary: The Jai Hind sound and light show tells the Red Fort's story on its walls every evening except Mondays.
places.seoTitle: Red Fort Light and Sound Show (Jai Hind): Guide
places.seoDescription: The Jai Hind sound and light show at the Red Fort: every evening except Mondays, what it covers, and how to fit it into an Old Delhi day.

images.alt: The Red Fort's walls and domed pavilions lit up at night
images.caption: The Red Fort at night

overview.text:
Every evening except Mondays, the Jai Hind sound and light show brings the Red Fort's story to life with lights, music and narration on the fort itself. It's an easy way to end a day in Old Delhi after the fort, the Jama Masjid and Chandni Chowk.

The Red Fort itself is open 9:30 am to 4:30 pm and closed on Mondays, so plan the fort during the day and come back for the evening show, with dinner in the lanes of Chandni Chowk in between. The fort was the Mughal emperors' home for almost 200 years, and the show is a lively way to get that story before or after you walk through it.

items.body: Not on Mondays — the fort is closed.
Check show times and languages locally on the day.

places.name: Akshardham water show
places.summary: The 24-minute Sahaj Anand show of lasers, fountains and live actors at Akshardham's stepwell, after sunset.
places.seoTitle: Akshardham Water Show: Timings, Tickets & Tips
places.seoDescription: Sahaj Anand Water Show at Akshardham: 24 minutes after sunset, ₹110 adults / ₹80 children, in Hindi, and what to know before you go.

overview.text: As the light fades, Akshardham's giant stepwell becomes the stage for the Sahaj Anand Water Show: 24 minutes of lasers, video projections, underwater flames, fountains and live actors telling a story from the Kena Upanishad. The first show starts soon after sunset, and it's in Hindi.

items.title: Tickets
items.body: ₹110 adults (12+) and seniors; ₹80 children 4–11; under-4s free.

items.title: Timing
items.body: First show soon after sunset; more on weekends and holidays.

items.title: Closed
items.body: Akshardham is closed on Mondays.

items.title: Note
items.body: On windy days you may get splashed.

places.name: Iftar at the Jama Masjid
places.summary: During Ramzan, join the crowds in the Jama Masjid's courtyard as the city's Muslims break their fast at sunset.
places.seoTitle: Iftar at Jama Masjid Delhi: What to Expect
places.seoDescription: Experience iftar at the Jama Masjid during Ramzan: what happens at sunset, etiquette for visitors, getting there by metro, and food in the lanes around.

images.alt: People sitting in rows on the floor of the Jama Masjid's arched cloister, preparing to break their fast
images.caption: Iftar at the Jama Masjid

overview.text:
Ramzan is the ninth month of the Islamic calendar, when Muslims fast through the day and break the fast after sunset with iftar — traditionally with dates and water first. At the Jama Masjid the courtyard fills with families on their mats, food spread out, waiting for the call that marks sunset. Heritage groups organise iftar gatherings that visitors can join.

If you're not fasting, it's polite not to eat or drink inside before sunset. Expect touts and people asking for alms on the steps.

how_to_reach.text: Take the metro to Jama Masjid station on the Violet Line's underground heritage stretch; the mosque is a short walk from Gate 1.

items.body: Ramzan falls on different dates every year — check them before you plan.
Dress modestly and cover your arms and legs.

places.name: Change of Guard at Rashtrapati Bhavan
places.summary: The President's Bodyguard and band in full ceremonial dress on the Forecourt of Rashtrapati Bhavan, on Saturday mornings.
places.seoTitle: Change of Guard at Rashtrapati Bhavan: Booking & Timing
places.seoDescription: Watch the Change of Guard at Rashtrapati Bhavan: Saturdays 8–9 am from 7 November 2026, ₹50 online registration, Gate 38 entry, Central Secretariat metro.

images.commons: File:Change of Guards at Rashtrapati Bhavan, New Delhi (29138604704).jpg
images.alt: Guards in red turbans and dress uniform marching, with a mounted bodyguard and fountain behind
images.caption: Change of Guard, Rashtrapati Bhavan

overview.text:
On Saturday mornings the guard at Rashtrapati Bhavan changes in full ceremony on the Forecourt. The President's Bodyguard — raised in 1773 and the senior-most regiment of the Indian Army — rides in on horseback to the Army brass band, the new guard takes over, and the ceremony ends with an equestrian display.

You must register online in advance (₹50 a person) and enter through Gate 38 on Church Road; Central Secretariat metro is about 1 km away. Arrive early for security checks, and combine it with a main-building tour or the museum, which open later the same morning.

items.title: When
items.body: Saturdays except gazetted holidays; 8–9 am from 7 November 2026.

items.title: Booking
items.body: Register online; ₹50 a person, non-refundable.

items.title: Entry
items.body: Gate 38, Church Road; Central Secretariat metro is about 1 km away.

places.name: Qawwali at the Nizamuddin Dargah
places.summary: Sufi devotional music at the shrine of Nizamuddin Auliya, every evening after sunset prayers and biggest on Thursday nights.
places.seoTitle: Qawwali at Nizamuddin Dargah: When to Go
places.seoDescription: Hear qawwali at Hazrat Nizamuddin Dargah: every evening after the Maghrib prayer, the big Thursday-night session, and how to visit respectfully.

images.alt: Qawwali singers with harmoniums performing to a seated crowd under strings of lights at Nizamuddin Dargah
images.caption: Qawwali at Nizamuddin Dargah

overview.text:
The dargah of the 13th-century Sufi saint Nizamuddin Auliya draws thousands of pilgrims a week, and it is famous for qawwali — devotional songs sung every evening after the Maghrib (sunset) prayer. The Thursday-night session is the biggest, with around 1,500 people.

Walk in through the lanes of Nizamuddin Basti; the tomb of the poet Amir Khusrau, the saint's disciple, is at the entrance. Humayun's Tomb and Sunder Nursery are a short walk away, so the qawwali makes a good end to a day of Mughal monuments. Arrive before sunset to find a place to sit; on Thursdays the courtyard is packed.

items.body: Dress modestly and cover your head; leave shoes at the stalls by the entrance.
Thursday evening is the most atmospheric — and the most crowded.

itineraries.title: Two days in Delhi: Old Delhi and the Mughal monuments
itineraries.summary: Day one in Old Delhi — the Red Fort, Jama Masjid and Chandni Chowk; day two from Humayun's Tomb to India Gate and the Qutub Minar.
itineraries.seoTitle: 2 Days in Delhi Itinerary: Old Delhi to Qutub Minar
itineraries.seoDescription: A realistic two-day Delhi itinerary: the Red Fort, Jama Masjid and Chandni Chowk, then Humayun's Tomb, India Gate and the Qutub Minar, with metro tips and timings.

Day 1 covers Old Delhi; Day 2 covers the Mughal and colonial monuments of New Delhi and the south. Don't start on a Monday: the Red Fort is closed that day — swap the days if you need to.

guides.title: How to reach Delhi: airport, trains and buses explained
guides.summary: Which airport terminal, which of Delhi's five railway stations, and which bus terminal you'll use — and the fastest ways into the city from each.
guides.seoTitle: How to Reach Delhi: Airport, Railway Stations & Buses
guides.seoDescription: Getting to Delhi: IGI airport terminals and the Airport Express metro, New Delhi, Old Delhi, Nizamuddin and Anand Vihar stations, and Kashmere Gate ISBT buses.

body.intro: Delhi is India's biggest transport hub, so getting here is easy — the trick is knowing which terminal or station you'll arrive at, because they're far apart.

sections.heading: By air
sections.text: Indira Gandhi International Airport, at Palam about 15 km south-west of New Delhi station, has been India's busiest airport since 2009. Two budget domestic airlines use Terminals 1 and 2; every other airline uses Terminal 3, which opened in 2010 and handles international flights. Check your terminal on your ticket. Noida International Airport at Jewar opened its first phase in March 2026.

items.title: Airport Express metro
items.body: The fastest link: about 15 minutes from the airport to New Delhi station, roughly 5 am to 11:40 pm, every 10–15 minutes.

items.title: Taxis and apps
items.body: Uber, Ola and Rapido operate; late at night be wary of drivers who target tired arrivals.

sections.heading: By train
sections.text: Delhi has five main stations: New Delhi (next to Paharganj), Old Delhi (the oldest, from 1864, linked to Chandni Chowk metro), Hazrat Nizamuddin, Anand Vihar Terminal (most east-bound trains, to UP and Bihar) and Sarai Rohilla. Check which one your train uses — they are an hour apart in traffic.

sections.heading: By bus
sections.text: Long-distance buses to Himachal Pradesh (Shimla, Manali), Uttarakhand, Punjab, Jammu & Kashmir and Rajasthan use Kashmere Gate ISBT, India's oldest interstate bus terminal, on the Yellow Line.

sections.heading: Avoid the station scams
sections.text: Touts around railway stations steer visitors to fake 'ticket offices for foreigners'. You never need a 'boarding pass' to enter a station — walk straight in.

checklist: Check your terminal (T1, T2 or T3) on your ticket
Check which station your train uses
Use the Airport Express metro if you land between 5 am and 11:30 pm

body.intro: Delhi is huge and its roads are jammed, so the metro is your best friend. Here's how to use it — and what to do for the bits it doesn't reach.

sections.text: Uber, Ola and Rapido fill the gaps. With auto-rickshaws, agree the fare or insist on the meter before you get in; even the prepaid desk at Old Delhi station has been known to charge well over its posted rates.

sections.heading: Old Delhi
sections.text: Take the metro to the edge of the old city, then walk or hop on a cycle rickshaw — it's the most fun way through the narrow lanes.

Check the AQI daily; if you have asthma or a heart condition, plan indoor sights on bad days.
